content:
Since 2010, AI models have grown at an extraordinary rate in terms of the number of parameters. Around 2010, the most advanced NLP models typically had only a few million parameters.

Then the acceleration began:
• 2018 - GPT-1: ~117 million parameters
• 2020 - GPT-3: ~175 billion parameters
• 2023 - GPT-4: estimated at ~1-1.8 trillion parameters

In just over a decade, we’ve moved from systems with millions of parameters to pioneering models with trillions of parameters. And the next step is even more striking;

Projections suggest that by 2030, AI systems will reach a scale of 10–100 trillion active parameters.

This means that many of the jobs we have today will become AI-native. I don’t know if AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) will be around by then, but many of us will either no longer be in our current jobs or will be doing our jobs in very different ways. Yes, in less than five years...

And below is the response GPT-5.5 gave me when I asked it to generate a visual interpretation of this scenario. The last line certainly made me smile. 😊

content:
One of the biggest unsolved problems in AI agents is memory.

Most systems today try to solve it by expanding the context window:
128K → 1M → even larger. (fyi: DeepSeek AI/DeepSeek-V4-Flash)

But this paper argues something important:
Bigger context does not automatically create better memory.

"They achieved meaningful gains using only an 8×8 memory state." - I was pretty surprised when I read that part. 😅

Check this out:
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.12357

content:
In the past, when using AI, we operated on a “one prompt, one response” model, and this didn’t impose excessive costs on AI providers. But in modern agentic workflows, capabilities such as:

- Planning
- Reflection
- Verification
- Retrieval
- Subagents
- Memory retrieval
- Reasoning loops, and so on, are becoming standard. And the cost of this has started to become truly burdensome for the companies providing these services.

I recommend reading: https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/ai-subscription-time-bomb

And believe me, the $20 we pay to OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google for ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini is nothing compared to the cost of these capabilities!

It might not be very soon, but in the near future, we’ll likely be discussing and budgeting for monthly fees of $100—or even $1,000—for AI tools we can’t live without.

My advice to you is to visit Hugging Face at least once a day and start researching how to build your own LLM systems now. Because when that day comes, you’ll have no choice but to do it.

content:
There used to be a significant performance gap between open-source models and proprietary models.

Today, that’s no longer the case. They still haven’t managed to win my full trust, but according to many reports, open-source models are no longer just a “cost-effective alternative”; they’ve reached a level where they can be preferred in a production environment under the right circumstances.

The link also highlights the idea that “the trend is no longer about choosing a model, but about model orchestration.” I think this topic is still very much open to debate. Because the "/compact" command you use with one model can lead to very different results for another model. This is just one specific example; I could give many others like it.

Regardless of the article, I don’t think I’m at the point where I could give up on Anthropic's Claude Code just yet. Yes, there have been notable developments on the application side, but Claude Code currently offers a truly solid solution. I say this because, while keeping up with developments is very important and implementing them is crucial, I’m always in favor of sticking with the stable release.

linkPreview.title: The State of Open-Source AI
linkPreview.description: An analysis of how open-source AI models have narrowed the performance gap with proprietary models, arguing that competitive advantage is increasingly shifting from model selection to orchestration, infrastructure, and production-ready AI systems.
